name: Venn region reading
statement: \text{Mark the regions inside exactly the required shapes and outside the excluded ones, then read or add their numbers.}
derivation: Name every region by the shapes it lies in (Teacher only, Teacher and Engineer only, all three).
Translate the question: 'more than one' = regions in 2 or 3 shapes; 'only X' = inside X and no other shape.
'X but not Y' = every region inside X and outside Y.
Add the numbers in the chosen regions, and no others.
visual_proof: The three circles cut the plane into seven numbered regions; each question is a union of some of them.

steps: 'More than one post' = regions in two or three circles.

common_traps: Leaving out the centre (all three) for 'more than one': $4+6+8 = 18$ instead of 21.
Adding every number inside a shape when 'only' was asked.
Counting the centre twice when adding two overlaps.
Adding all regions (154) or only the single-post regions (133) when overlaps are asked.

diagram.alt_text: Three overlapping circles Teacher, Engineer, Accountant with region counts: Teacher only 35, Engineer only 42, Accountant only 56, Teacher and Engineer 4, Teacher and Accountant 6, Engineer and Accountant 8, all three 3.

verification.code:
def region_sum(regions, inside_count=None, need=(), exclude=()):
    """regions: {frozenset of sets: count}. Sum the regions inside every 'need' set, outside every
    'exclude' set, and (optionally) inside exactly/at least a number of sets."""
    total = 0
    for key, v in regions.items():
        if not set(need) <= key or key & set(exclude):
            continue
        if inside_count and not inside_count(len(key)):
            continue
        total += v
    return total

R = lambda *s: frozenset(s)
# Worked example 2024-09-09_1600_R09 (Teacher, Engineer, Accountant), counts read off the figure
fig = {R("T"): 35, R("E"): 42, R("A"): 56, R("T", "E"): 4, R("T", "A"): 6, R("E", "A"): 8, R("T", "E", "A"): 3}
more_than_one = region_sum(fig, inside_count=lambda k: k >= 2)
assert more_than_one == 21
options = {"A": 21, "B": 15, "C": 113, "D": 18}
assert [k for k, v in options.items() if v == more_than_one] == ["A"]
# Traps give the wrong options: two-only overlaps 18, leaving out the centre
assert region_sum(fig, inside_count=lambda k: k == 2) == 18
# Same figure: exactly one post, teachers who are not accountants, all three
assert region_sum(fig, inside_count=lambda k: k == 1) == 133
assert region_sum(fig, need=["T"], exclude=["A"]) == 39
assert region_sum(fig, need=["T", "E", "A"]) == 3

name: Best-fit Venn diagram
statement: \text{For each pair of classes decide: one inside the other, overlap, or disjoint; choose the diagram that shows all pairs that way.}
derivation: List every pair: three classes give three pairs.
For each pair ask: is every X a Y (inside), can some be both (overlap), or none (disjoint)?
Write the pattern, e.g. Mothers inside Women; Doctors overlaps Women; Doctors overlaps Mothers.
Pick the option whose circles match all three pairs, not just two.
visual_proof: Women as a large circle with Mothers inside it, and Doctors as a circle cutting across both.
common_traps: Drawing Doctors inside Women because many doctors are women; some are men, so they overlap.
Making Doctors and Mothers disjoint; a mother can be a doctor.
Matching two pairs and ignoring the third.
Drawing Dogs and Cats as overlapping inside Animals; no animal is both.

diagram.alt_text: Women, Mothers, Doctors: the Mothers circle lies inside Women; the Doctors circle crosses both, so Mothers outside Women is empty.
